result:
Split-K=4 is fastest, at about 25.3 µs. The times below come from the simulator's `gemm_tiling` tool.

With M=16, a 128×128 tile gives only 64 output tiles, so split-K=1 launches 64 CTAs on 148 SMs. Its time is 35.8 µs, which is memory-latency-bound, with 57% of the SMs idle. Splitting K adds CTAs and puts more bytes in flight, so the weight stream gets close to the HBM roof.

| split-K | CTAs | CTAs per SM | Time (µs) | Bound |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 64 | 1 | 35.8 | memory latency |
| 2 | 128 | 1 | 27.1 | HBM |
| 4 | 256 | 2 | 25.3 | HBM |
| 8 | 512 | 2 | 26.8 | HBM |

Split-K=4 reaches about 5.4 TB/s, roughly 79% of achievable HBM bandwidth. Split-K=8 loses time because it needs 1.73 waves and adds partial-sum traffic (170 MB of DRAM traffic against 153 MB).

The simulator's error band on this result is about ±4% from the per-variant measurement, and 12% in the summary band. The roofline floor is about 20.4 µs.
